title: Jimmy Review: KJ Apa’s Flawed Attempt to Revive James Stewart’s Dutiful Biopic Falls Short
body:
The new limited series “Jimmy,” starring KJ Apa as the legendary Hollywood icon, attempts to illuminate the lesser‑known wartime chapter of James Stewart’s life, but critics argue that the production’s reverent tone and conventional storytelling ultimately hinder its ambition to reshape the actor’s mythos. While the drama benefits from authentic period details and the involvement of Stewart’s own daughter, Mary Stewart, as an executive producer, the series struggles to move beyond a safe, biographical tribute and fails to capture the complexity that made Stewart a cultural touchstone.

“Jimmy” chronicles the Academy‑Award‑winning star’s service as a bomber pilot and later as a morale‑boosting officer during World II, a period that profoundly influenced his post‑war career. The six‑hour narrative follows Stewart from his enlistment in 1941 through his return to Hollywood, interweaving combat sequences with personal moments that aim to reveal the man behind the screen‑friendly persona. Apa, best known for his brooding turn as Archie Murray on “Riverdale,” brings a youthful earnestness to the role, attempting to embody Stewart’s trademark integrity and understated charisma.

The series’ production values are undeniably high‑caliber. Meticulously recreated 1940s airfields, authentic flight gear, and a muted color palette evoke the era’s stark realities, while a subtle score underscores the tension of aerial combat without overwhelming the drama. Moreover, Mary Stewart’s participation lends an aura of legitimacy, ensuring that family archives and personal anecdotes inform the storytelling. Interviews with the actress reveal a desire to honor her father’s “quiet heroism” and to showcase a side of him that the public rarely sees.

However, the very reverence that underpins the series also becomes its Achilles’ heel. Reviewers note that the narrative adheres too closely to a conventional, almost documentary‑like structure, offering little in the way of dramatic risk or nuanced character study. Apa’s performance, while competent, often feels restrained, mirroring Stewart’s famously restrained screen presence but lacking the inner conflict that would make the wartime hero more relatable to contemporary audiences. Scenes intended to probe Stewart’s moral dilemmas—such as his decision to continue flying combat missions after his first harrowing loss—are presented with a straightforward, almost didactic clarity that leaves little room for interpretive depth.

The series also contends with the challenge of balancing historical fidelity with narrative momentum. While the inclusion of authentic combat footage and period‑accurate dialogue enriches the viewing experience, the pacing suffers during extended sequences of military briefing and procedural routine. Critics argue that these moments, though historically accurate, could have been trimmed or dramatized to maintain viewer engagement. In contrast, the more intimate domestic scenes—showing Stewart’s interactions with his wife, Gloria Holland, and his children—provide fleeting glimpses of emotional resonance, suggesting that a tighter focus on personal stakes might have yielded a more compelling portrait.

Despite its shortcomings, “Jimmy” arrives at a time when audiences are eager for nuanced depictions of World II veterans, especially those whose contributions extended beyond the battlefield. The series contributes to a growing body of work that seeks to humanize iconic figures, reminding viewers that celebrated actors like Stewart were also ordinary men thrust into extraordinary circumstances. Its respectful tone may appeal to older viewers and Stewart’s admirers, while younger audiences might find the measured pacing less engaging.

Looking ahead, the show’s reception could influence how future biopics handle the delicate balance between homage and critical inquiry. If “Jimmy” spurs renewed interest in Stewart’s wartime service, it may inspire more daring explorations of his post‑war political activism and his complex relationship with Hollywood’s evolving culture. For now, the series stands as a well‑intentioned, if overly cautious, tribute—one that honors a beloved star’s legacy while reminding creators that even the most dignified subjects benefit from a narrative that dares to ask uncomfortable questions.
